title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Solar panel cleaning
audience: Solar panel cleaning owners and team leads who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a panel cleaning need may be starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what panel work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the array sizes you clean well, the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each client needs you. A route of homes you can reach in one day, with safe access and a clear water supply, is worth more to a small business than a single large job across town. No current evidence in this research shows how often panels are cleaned, so the repeat need must be tested in your own area.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list, and be plain about the evidence
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using written criteria: service area, repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the job falls within your licence and insurance. Candidate segments include installers, electricians who service systems, real-estate offices, warranty providers and owners corporations with solar on common property. This research found no evidence of installer or warranty-provider referral agreements, no real-estate evidence and no evidence that any of these segments buys panel cleaning. Treat each as a segment to test. Use only contact details published for business use, record the date and source of each entry, and do not use bought or harvested lists.

instruction.heading: Use public signals for timing only, and do not build a list from enforcement news
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. Public registers, such as the City of Casey planning permit register on Victoria's open data portal, show application status and suburb; check your own council's register. Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts. WorkSafe Victoria publishes news about solar companies, including prosecutions and fines. Those releases describe fall-protection failures; they are not a list of clients for panel cleaning, and approaching a company because it has been prosecuted would be a poor first approach. Do not monitor private people, do not enter a property without an invitation, and do not go to a home to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you learned of the business or notice, makes one specific observation you can verify from public view or the business's own published material, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for one named array. Keep it short and do not overstate what you know. The ACCC's July 2026 release on unsolicited selling found many approaches were pressured or misleading, that about 80 per cent of respondents said unsolicited selling seldom gave useful information or offers, and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves. A specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage. Where the message goes by email or text, check the consent and unsubscribe rules first.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, then a pause. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work, and move your effort toward them.

procedure: Write the array size, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and the source of its contact details.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and your licence and insurance before sending. Remove any electrical service from the message.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A solar panel cleaner reads a public WorkSafe Victoria release about an installer that was fined after inspectors found workers without adequate fall protection. The cleaner considers contacting the installer to offer cleaning services straight away.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the cleaner make contact now, and what should any message contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The release is a public enforcement notice about fall protection. It is not an invitation to sell, and a sales approach that refers to a prosecution would be poor judgement. The cleaner checks whether the business publishes contact details for business use, and whether a specific, honest offer fits its needs. Any message that does go out is short, says how the cleaner learned of the business, does not refer to the fine, and offers one small next step, such as a written note on the cleaner's own method for water-only cleaning. The cleaner does not offer electrical work, does not use private contact details of staff, and does not present the cleaning as a fall-protection service unless the Victorian rule has been checked and the cleaner is able to meet it.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the Victorian working-at-height method and the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Offering electrical work or fall-protection services you are not licensed or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. The licence scope for panel cleaning was not researched. Electrical servicing requires a licensed electrician (Solar Victoria). This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Public information does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Act applies to a small business is unconfirmed here.

Victoria: the working-at-height rule for roof access was not checked in this draft. WorkSafe Victoria says allowing workers onto a roof without adequate protection is unlawful, even with no incident, and Solar Victoria says installers that fail to provide basic fall protection face suspension or cancellation. Check the Victorian rule before quoting any roof access.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step, and no electrical service is offered.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the panel work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals for timing, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline. Installer, warranty-provider and real-estate prospects are untested for cleaning work.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public enforcement release names a solar company fined for fall-protection failures. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Check whether the company publishes a business contact route, and whether a specific, honest offer fits, before any message is sent
Message the company's staff using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for cleaning
Go to the company's installation sites to look at the panels before making contact

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include a free unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. Does not cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act, which covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some others. The page as read lists the APP chapters only; small-business coverage and consent detail are UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: OAIC.
